resident.chief_complaint: Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months in a 41-year-old female with no history of trauma.
resident.history: A 41-year-old female with no history of trauma presented with weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction over the last 2 months. Initial cervical noncontrast MRI showed a hyperintense intramedullary cord signal, with differential diagnoses including cervical spondylotic myelopathy and tumor. She was referred for an open biopsy of the cervical spinal cord to document the pathology of the tumor. At the time of transfer, she had severe spastic quadriparesis, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Follow-up MRI revealed cervical spondylosis with C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression associated with an extensive intramedullary high cord signal and cord enlargement on T2-weighted sagittal images extending from C5 to C7; axial images confirmed the intramedullary signal abnormality. T1-weighted MRI sagittal scan showed the lesion enhanced with contrast at the C5–C6 level.
resident.physical_exam: On examination at the time of transfer, severe spastic quadriparesis was present, markedly greater in the upper than in the lower extremities. Weakness and numbness involving all four extremities and progressive sphincter dysfunction were reported in the history. Detailed motor power, reflexes, sensation, and sphincter examination findings are not documented in the record.

red_flags.finding: Intramedullary cord enlargement and contrast enhancement at C5–C6 on MRI
red_flags.rationale: This suggests an intrinsic cord lesion (e.g., tumor, demyelination, inflammation) that could independently cause the progressive myelopathy; surgical decompression for spondylotic compression may not address the primary pathology, and biopsy or medical management may be needed.

In compressive cervical myelopathy from C5–C7 spondylosis, lower extremities are typically more affected due to longer corticospinal tracts; upper extremity predominance suggests a central cord or intramedullary process, reinforcing the likelihood of a primary cord lesion rather than compression alone.

neurology.symptom_imaging_mismatch: The imaging shows C5–C6 and C6–C7 cord compression, but the clinical pattern of upper extremity-predominant spastic quadriparesis is atypical for compressive cervical myelopathy at those levels, which would be expected to affect lower limbs more; additionally, cord enlargement and contrast enhancement are not typical for simple spondylotic compression, suggesting an intramedullary lesion that better explains the symptoms.

preconditions_for_failure: No improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of intensive conservative therapy.

Inability to participate in therapy due to pain, functional decline, or medical instability.
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I remain the strongest advocate for conservative care. Given the progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, surgery is being considered, but before proceeding to irreversible intervention, I propose a formal, time-limited 3-6 month trial of intensive conservative management under close neurological monitoring. This would include supervised physical therapy for gait/balance/strength, occupational therapy for activities of daily living, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, and avoidance of high-risk activities. The literature on nonoperative management of cervical spondylotic myelopathy reports that a subset of patients—particularly those with mild symptoms and no rapid progression—can stabilize or improve without surgery; however, I acknowledge that severe spastic quadriparesis with sphincter involvement and cord enhancement indicates a poorer prognosis for conservative care. Therefore, I define failure as any of the following: (1) no improvement or further deterioration in motor or sphincter function after 3 months of strict conservative therapy; (2) new or worsening neurological deficits during the trial; (3) progression of intramedullary signal abnormality or enhancement on follow-up MRI at 3 months; or (4) inability to participate in therapy due to pain or functional decline. If any of these occur, I will accept that conservative management has failed and support surgical intervention or biopsy as appropriate. Until then, I hold my stance for a trial of conservative care.

physiatrist_final.public_message: I remain conditional. The Director and Deputy have reiterated the severe progressive myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction, but these are findings I already weighed heavily when I accepted urgent surgery if an intrinsic tumor is confirmed. They have not pointed to any new finding that I underweighted; the risk of irreversible progression from a neoplastic lesion was the very reason I moved from hold to conditional. I agree with the Director's plan for further imaging to distinguish tumor from non-neoplastic causes—that is appropriate and may refine the decision. However, if the repeat MRI and biopsy ultimately show no neoplasm and the pathology is purely spondylotic, a brief, closely monitored conservative trial remains a reasonable option before committing to definitive decompression. The window for conservative management is narrowing given the documented progression and sphincter involvement, but it is not closed until the nature of the enhancing lesion is clarified. Therefore, I hold at conditional: I support urgent surgery if an intrinsic tumor is confirmed or if repeat imaging shows no likely non-surgical diagnosis; otherwise, I advocate for a time-limited trial with strict failure criteria as previously outlined.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old woman with rapidly progressive cervical myelopathy (spastic quadriparesis, upper extremity predominant, sphincter dysfunction) and MRI evidence of cord compression at C5-6 and C6-7 with an enhancing intramedullary lesion at C5-6. The enhancement and cord enlargement raise the possibility of an intrinsic cord tumor, but spondylotic compression with myelomalacia can also produce enhancement. Regardless of the underlying cause, the severe and progressive deficits with sphincter involvement represent a surgical emergency; a 3-6 month conservative trial would risk irreversible spinal cord injury. I recommend urgent surgical decompression, with intraoperative assessment and possible biopsy of any intrinsic lesion.
proposed_options: Urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF or corpectomy as indicated by compression anatomy) at C5-6 and C6-7, with intraoperative ultrasound; if an intrinsic cord lesion is identified, proceed with biopsy if safely feasible.

Posterior cervical decompression (laminectomy or laminoplasty) if the compression is predominantly posterior or if a multi-level decompression is needed; can be combined with biopsy of any dorsal intrinsic lesion.

Short-term high-dose corticosteroid treatment followed by repeat contrast-enhanced MRI in 2-4 weeks to reassess the enhancing lesion before committing to surgery; this delays definitive treatment and is not my preference, but may be considered if the director wants further diagnostic clarity.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF or corpectomy as indicated) with intraoperative ultrasound and biopsy of any intrinsic cord lesion.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's proposal for a 3-6 month conservative trial: severe progressive myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction is an indication for urgent surgical decompression; a conservative trial carries unacceptable risk of permanent cord damage.

The enhancing intramedullary lesion cannot be dismissed as simple reactive change; it may represent an intrinsic cord tumor, which would not be adequately treated by decompression alone. This needs to be addressed intraoperatively or with targeted imaging, not by observation.

Upper extremity-predominant weakness is atypical for compression-only myelopathy and supports the possibility of intrinsic cord pathology; however, this does not justify delaying decompression, as compression is also present.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed directly to surgery, or obtain additional preoperative imaging (e.g., contrast-enhanced MRI with fat suppression, CT myelogram, or CSF analysis) to better characterize the enhancing lesion?
If surgery is chosen, do you favor the anterior approach (ACDF/corpectomy) versus a posterior decompression, given the two-level compression and cord enlargement?
If an intrinsic cord lesion is encountered intraoperatively, should biopsy be performed in the same setting, or should it be staged after decompression?
vice_opinions.public_message: My assessment is severe progressive cervical myelopathy with sphincter dysfunction, likely from cord compression at C5-6 and C6-7, but the enhancing intramedullary lesion raises concern for an intrinsic cord tumor. I recommend urgent surgical decompression rather than conservative therapy; waiting 3-6 months risks irreversible neurologic decline. My preference is anterior decompression and fusion with intraoperative ultrasound and biopsy if an intrinsic lesion is identified. I disagree with the conservative trial and raise the questions of whether additional preoperative imaging is needed and how to handle the enhancing lesion intraoperatively.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 41-year-old with severe progressive cervical myelopathy and sphincter dysfunction. Imaging shows two-level cord compression from spondylosis at C5-6 and C6-7, but also an extensive intramedullary T2 hyperintense lesion and contrast enhancement at C5-6. The upper-extremity-predominant weakness and sphincter involvement are more typical of an intrinsic cord lesion than pure spondylotic myelopathy. Urgent surgical intervention is warranted, but the enhancing lesion must be characterized to avoid an inappropriate procedure. I agree with the plan for repeat high-resolution contrast MRI and input from radiology and the resident before finalizing the approach.
proposed_options: Proceed with urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion at C5-6 and C6-7, with intraoperative ultrasound and biopsy of any enhancing lesion; if frozen section suggests tumor, terminate and refer for staged oncologic management.

Proceed with posterior cervical laminectomy/laminoplasty and open biopsy of the intramedullary lesion, which provides direct access for tissue diagnosis and decompresses the cord; add instrumented fusion if instability results.
Complete repeat high-resolution MRI and consultant reviews before surgery, then choose the approach based on those findings; this avoids an inappropriate procedure but adds a short delay.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Proceed with urgent anterior cervical decompression and fusion at C5-6 and C6-7, with intraoperative ultrasound and biopsy of any enhancing lesion; if frozen section suggests tumor, terminate and refer for staged oncologic management.
disagreement_points: The relative contribution of spondylotic compression versus intrinsic cord lesion to the myelopathy remains unresolved; the upper-extremity-predominant weakness and enhancement should not be dismissed.
Whether an anterior approach can safely biopsy an intramedullary lesion at C5-6 is uncertain; a posterior approach may be required if the lesion is dorsal or extensive.
The role of a short course of high-dose steroids if inflammatory myelitis is in the differential has not been settled, as it could affect timing and intraoperative findings.
deferred_questions_to_director: Do you want a neurosurgical or oncologic consultation before finalizing the approach, or is intraoperative decision-making sufficient?
If repeat MRI strongly suggests demyelination or inflammatory myelitis, would you consider a short trial of high-dose steroids or further medical workup before surgery?
